accuracy.reason: All nine objectives checked against every linked page and targeted primary followups. Replacement semantics, conditional-write scope, retry uncertainty, duplicate retention, eventual TTL removal, capacity eviction and durability/read visibility are correctly separated. Generic model teaching is not misrepresented as a universal DynamoDB feature set.

evidence.quote: Repeating the same operation leaves the same result. Replacing a value with the identical value twice does this if no other write intervenes. Executing an increment twice adds twice, even if each increment is individually atomic.

An expiration rule for an entry. Check when the product stops returning expired data and when it physically removes it. For example, DynamoDB's background TTL deletion can leave expired items readable while deletion is pending.

mechanisms.reason: Clear key-to-value access and replacement trace, collision example, scan/index maintenance, lost-update interleaving and atomic conflict retry. The operation-ID crash boundary and TTL/eviction aftermath are explicit. Namespace and version-check diagrams preserve both authorization and concurrency limitations.

evidence.quote: Two callers read a count of 10. Each adds one locally and puts 11. Both writes can succeed, but the final count is 11 instead of 12. One intended increment is lost.

Only one update based on the old version succeeds. The rejected caller rereads the current value and version, recomputes its change and makes another conditional attempt. Bound retries when contention persists.

coherence.reason: Known-key identity and operations precede value/key design and alternate queries; concurrency precedes retry safety, then entry lifetime and distribution inform the final selection. Every objective is taught with prerequisites rather than relying on learner knowledge of sharding, transactions or cache behavior.

evidence.quote: A key-value store can hold authoritative data, the record the application treats as its source of truth. It can also hold a disposable copy of data kept elsewhere. That second role is caching; the access model does not decide the role.
A portion of the keyspace assigned to a storage node or group. Distributing different key groups can spread their storage and request work.

decisions.reason: Guides value boundary and identity encoding, permission checks, scan/index tradeoffs, conditional update versus blind overwrite, uncertain-increment recovery, authoritative retention and workload fit. Costs and product-specific failure guarantees accompany benefits; it identifies when richer query support fits better.

evidence.quote: An index takes storage and update work. When a record moves cities or is deleted, the index must change too. Check who maintains it and when its results reflect writes; an application-maintained index adds coordination work.

Joins combine related records. Frequent joins or new filters over value fields need more than basic key lookup. Scans read extra data; indexes and duplicated records add update work; application-side joins add requests and coordination.

clarity.reason: Definitions and numerical examples make the required distinctions usable, and the actual learner transfers them correctly. The unintroduced term backoff and abstract instruction to reconcile through an application recovery path make the retry card less self-contained than the otherwise precise prose. This is a clarity limitation, not an omitted required recovery algorithm or objective.

evidence.quote: Without verified duplicate protection, do not blindly repeat the uncertain increment. Reconcile its outcome through an application recovery path. Use bounded retry/backoff for retryable failures; retrying every error can worsen an outage.
Use an unambiguous encoding of those parts. A separator is safe only if values cannot contain it or are escaped consistently. Every caller must construct the same identity the same way.

outcomes.reason: Defines known-key access, supplies escaped tenant/device/record-kind tuple and complete settings value; distinguishes authoritative from cached role and unproven durability. Correctly traces whole replacement losing color, deletion-observing absence versus timed-out unknown, and independent authorization. Exact quotes and slide3 boundary paragraph support all five criteria.

Explains why region is not the equipment key, scan inspection cost and post-read filtering, alternate region-to-ID access plus record fetch, and index storage/update/visibility responsibility. Checks actual store support instead of asserting universal indexes; all four criteria satisfied.

Correctly computes lost count21 rather than22. One version7 condition-and-write succeeds; rejected writer rereads current state and recomputes22 before retrying. Separate check retains the race. Not assigning an exact new version is acceptable: the criterion requires changed version, not a specified numbering algorithm.

All six criteria met: uncertain execution, identical replacement only under no intervening-write assumption, increment duplicate risk, stable-intent operation recognition with atomic record/effect and retention or avoidance of blind retry, expiry versus capacity eviction, and no retention/refresh/timed-work promise. Product scope and configuration checked; no nonexistent recovery implementation is invented.

Defines partition without assumed sharding knowledge, explains distributed key groups versus single-key serving bottleneck, distinguishes allowed stale replica reads from acknowledged-data survival, and checks implementation/persistence/replication/read-write modes before guarantees. Exact slide8 quotations support all five criteria.

A matches known-key independent replacement; B incurs scans/index updates/application-join requests and coordination. Chooses authorization and atomic concurrent-update protection for A and explains each concrete failure prevented. Rejects speed/safety by label and calls for representative measurements; all four criteria satisfied.

sourceChecks.claim: DynamoDB core components verifies unique keys and structured item values, with primary-key lookup. https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/ supplies the missing cross-product durability evidence through different persistence/fsync choices. Authoritative versus cache is an application role, not implied by key lookup.

GetItem distinguishes missing Item from returned data and operational errors. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_PutItem.html explicitly verifies whole-item replacement and permitted empty non-key attributes; delete/read visibility is correctly conditional. A timeout is lack of response, not a missing-item result.

Linked IAM conditions verifies per-item identity-based authorization, not automatic permission from a key. Core-components compound uniqueness and the general-design page support access-shaped values. Tenant/account/kind identity and unambiguous delimiter encoding are explicit collision-avoidance reasoning, not a claimed DynamoDB built-in encoding. Diagram distinguishes A/B identities and keeps permission separate.

AWS secondary-index page verifies alternate keys, projected primary keys, automated maintenance on writes/deletes, storage/write costs and consistency differences. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Scan.html confirms inspection before filtering and read-capacity consumption. Generic key-value access promises neither index nor range support.

Linked condition examples support conditional success/failure. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DynamoDBMapper.OptimisticLocking.html verifies expected-version match, version change, rejection and reread. Its global-table caveat reinforces the lesson requirement to verify scope; no universal cross-key or external-action safety is asserted. Diagram traces10/version4 to11/version5 and recomputation12.

AWS error guide explicitly says a failed-response write may have succeeded and requires state/condition checks before retries. https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/ requires ACID token-plus-mutation. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_TransactWriteItems.html specifies stable token, identical intent and ten-minute scope. Deck correctly requires actual support/retention rather than promising a universal feature.

AWS TTL says expired items await background deletion and can remain in query/scan results. https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/ verifies configurable memory-limit eviction, including entries with remaining TTL, or noeviction errors. Together these support separate lifetime/physical removal, no retention promise, no automatic source reload and no exact-time business execution.

Partition-key guidance confirms uniform request distribution, per-partition capacity and item-size effects. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html separately states durable200 writes and possibly stale eventual reads. Redis persistence documentation supplies the converse visibility-with-weaker-crash-survival example. More partitions alone need not disperse one key.

AWS design guidance requires identifying queries, data size/shape/velocity and avoiding concentrated load; secondary-index and scan docs show added access-path costs. Choosing richer queries/transactions for joins or changing filters is conditional, not a product ranking. Network/value/hot-key limits preclude speed or safety guarantees from the model alone.
